paragraphs: Born in Boston in 1823, Francis Parkman studied at Harvard and began planning a history of the struggle for North America. His writing brought together journeys through the country and the study of its documentary record, following the contest between France and England across the continent.

In 1846 he travelled from St. Louis into the Great Plains with his cousin Quincy Adams Shaw. Emigrant wagons, buffalo hunts, Fort Laramie and weeks among the Oglala supplied the material for his first book. The narrative appeared in the Knickerbocker Magazine before its publication as The California and Oregon Trail in 1849.

Parkman later became known for The Conspiracy of Pontiac and the series France and England in North America. The Discovery of the Great West, published in 1869 as the third part of that history, follows French exploration into the continental interior and La Salle’s journeys toward the Mississippi. Together, these books approach North America through the experiences of travellers and the ambitions of competing powers.
